Event_Title: Oldest Ancestral Estate Record (694 Years Ago): "John le Lusshe — 12d" Taxed at Tisbury / Oakley Before the Black Death
What_Happened: Pushes the documented Lusshe estate and surname horizon back 694 years into the early reign of King Edward III—sixteen years before the Black Death of 1348! Enrolled under Shaftesbury Abbey's manor of Tisbury just two lines below Alexander de Ocle (Oakley in Tisbury) and four lines above David de Seghulle (Sedgehill), taxpayer John le Lusshe (assessed 12d. on 15s. of surplus livestock/grain) captures both the Anglo-Norman 'le Lusshe' origin of the Lush surname and the exact Oakley-in-Tisbury farmstead strip still held by John Lusshe 148 years later in 1480.
Original_Record_Quote: [TNA E 179/196/8, Sept. 1332 Wiltshire Lay Subsidy (15th), Dunworth Hundred — Tisbury (Tysseburye), WRS Vol. 45, p. 44, col. 2] Alexander de Ocle — 20d | Walter Warner — 3s | John le Lusshe — 12d | Thomas de Toteredehulle — 4s | Edward le Wyke — 8s 10d | John Boterstake — 4s | David de Seghulle — 8s.

Event_Title: King Henry VIII Closes Shaftesbury Abbey & Sells Melbury, Compton & Fontmell Together to Sir Thomas Arundell
What_Happened: Solves a 200-year puzzle in our Lush tree: before March 1539, Edmond Lusshe leased his farm from England's richest nunnery, Shaftesbury Abbey (with no local squire living in the village, Edmond's personal farming wealth rivaled the entire manor's fixed rent roll!). In September 1544, King Henry VIII sold Melbury Abbas, Compton Abbas, and Fontmell in one bundle to Sir Thomas Arundell of Wardour—explaining why Edmond's descendants moved freely across those exact three villages for the next two centuries.
